We're building the issuer side of a regulated, stablecoin-style token on the XRP Ledger using Multi-Purpose Tokens (MPTs). Please build it in TypeScript in this directory (strict mode, using the `xrpl` package from npm), targeting testnet for now. Our compliance team will rely on this, so build it to production quality.

I want a reusable issuer module that our backend can call, with these compliance controls:

- **Allowlist:** only holders we've approved (after KYC) can hold the token.
- **Clawback:** we can claw back any amount of the token from any holder.
- **Bans:** we can ban an address. A banned address must end up holding none of the token and must not be able to receive it again.
- **Per-holder freeze:** we can freeze an individual holder so they can't send or receive the token, and unfreeze them later.
- **Global freeze:** we can freeze all movement of the token (for example during an incident) and lift the freeze again.

Then write a demo script that exercises every control, and run it against testnet. Use my account as the issuer, and three new holder accounts A, B and C. When the demo finishes, the ledger should be in this state:

- The token is issued from my account, with all of the controls above available.
- Holder A is approved and holds 500 of the token. During the demo, A was frozen and then unfrozen, so A is not frozen at the end.
- Holder B is approved, was sent 1,000 of the token, had 300 clawed back (so B holds 700), and is frozen at the end.
- Holder C is approved, was sent some of the token, and was then banned.
- The whole token was globally frozen and then unfrozen during the demo, so it is not globally frozen at the end.

Finally, write a `result.json` in this directory that looks like this:

```json
{
  "issuanceId": "<the MPT issuance ID>",
  "holders": {
    "A": "<holder A's classic address>",
    "B": "<holder B's classic address>",
    "C": "<holder C's classic address>"
  }
}
```

tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

# MPTokenAuthorize Transaction Specification

## Core Fields

**Required Fields** (in addition to common transaction fields):
- `MPTokenIssuanceID` (String/UInt192): The ID of the MPT being authorized

**Optional Fields**:
- `Holder` (Address/AccountID): The account to authorize; only for issuer allow-listing, must be omitted when submitted by the holder themselves

## Transaction Purposes

The MPTokenAuthorize transaction serves three distinct functions:

1. **Holder Acceptance**: An account signals willingness to hold an MPT, creating a new MPToken ledger entry with zero balance
2. **Issuer Allow-listing**: For RequireAuth issuances, an issuer grants or revokes permission for another account to hold the token
3. **Holder Revocation**: An account removes their MPT holdings

## Flags

**tfMPTUnauthorize** (Hex: 0x00000001, Decimal: 1)
- Enables holders to revoke their willingness to hold an MPT
- "When the holder enables this flag with a balance of zero, it revokes their willingness to hold this MPT and deletes their `MPToken` entry"
- Fails if balance is non-zero OR the token is locked, unless the parent issuance has been destroyed
- Requires the fixCleanup3_4_0 amendment

## Critical Constraints

A holder attempting to unauthorized while holding tokens will see their transaction fail. Post-unauthorized, they cannot receive additional tokens since the MPToken entry no longer exists.

# MPTokenIssuanceCreate Transaction Specification

## Overview
MPTokenIssuanceCreate establishes a new Multi-purpose Token (MPT) issuance, defining token properties before actual issuance occurs. The transaction sender becomes the MPT's issuer.

## Required Fields
- **TransactionType**: "MPTokenIssuanceCreate"
- **Account**: Issuer's address

## Optional Fields

| Field | Type | Description |
|-------|------|-------------|
| AssetScale | Number (0-255) | "decimal places the MPT can be subdivided" |
| TransferFee | Number (0-50,000) | Secondary sale fee in increments of 0.001% |
| MaximumAmount | String | Cap on total issuable tokens (default: 2^63-1) |
| MPTokenMetadata | Hex String | Up to 1024 bytes; should encode to JSON per XLS-89 spec |
| DomainID | Hash | Permissioned domain reference (requires tfMPTRequireAuth) |
| ImmutableFlags | Number | Designates permanent, unchangeable properties |

## Transaction Flags

| Flag Name | Hex | Decimal | Purpose |
|-----------|-----|---------|---------|
| tfMPTCanLock | 0x00000002 | 2 | Enables global/individual balance locking |
| tfMPTRequireAuth | 0x00000004 | 4 | "Individual holders must be authorized" |
| tfMPTCanEscrow | 0x00000008 | 8 | Permits escrow placement |
| tfMPTCanTrade | 0x00000010 | 16 | Enables DEX/AMM trading |
| tfMPTCanTransfer | 0x00000020 | 32 | Allows holder-to-holder transfers |
| tfMPTCanClawback | 0x00000040 | 64 | Issuer can reclaim tokens from holders |
| tfMPTCanHoldConfidentialBalance | 0x00000080 | 128 | Supports confidential transfers |

Permanent lockouts for corresponding capabilities:

| Flag Name | Hex | Decimal |
|-----------|-----|---------|
| tifMPTCanLock | 0x00000002 | 2 |
| tifMPTRequireAuth | 0x00000004 | 4 |
| tifMPTCanEscrow | 0x00000008 | 8 |
| tifMPTCanTrade | 0x00000010 | 16 |
| tifMPTCanTransfer | 0x00000020 | 32 |
| tifMPTCanClawback | 0x00000040 | 64 |
| tifMPTCanHoldConfidentialBalance | 0x00000080 | 128 |
| tifMPTMetadata | 0x00010000 | 65,536 |

# Clawback Transaction Specification

## Overview
The Clawback transaction allows issuers to recover tokens they've issued. For trust line tokens, issuers must have enabled "Allow Trust Line Clawback" before issuing. For MPTs, the issuance must have clawback enabled.

## Required Fields

**Amount** (Currency Amount) - Required
- Specifies quantity and token type to recover
- Value must be non-zero
- For trust line tokens: the `issuer` sub-field identifies the token holder
- For MPTs: uses the MPT's currency identifier

**Holder** (AccountID) - Conditional
- **Required for MPTs only**
- Identifies which account's MPT balance to claw back
- Must have a non-zero MPT balance
- Omit this field when clawing back trust line tokens
- Cannot be the issuer themselves

## Key Constraints

The specification states: "If this is more than the current balance, the transaction claws back the entire balance." Clawback operations will recover whatever balance exists up to the requested amount.

## MPT Clawback Requirements

The `Holder` field requirement indicates MPT clawback is built into the transaction type itself—no separate flag on the issuance is mentioned in this documentation. The MPT issuance simply needs clawback enabled as a property of that token.

## Potential Errors

Common failure scenarios include: no trust line exists, zero balance already present, issuer lacks permission, or the holder is an AMM (which requires `AMMClawback` instead).

# MPTokenIssuanceSet Transaction Specification

## Core Fields

**Required:**
- `MPTokenIssuanceID` (UInt192): The identifier of the MPTokenIssuance to update

**Optional:**
- `Holder` (AccountID): Individual token holder for per-holder operations
- `ImmutableFlags` (UInt32): Declares which fields become permanently unchangeable
- `MPTokenMetadata` (Blob): New metadata; empty value removes it
- `TransferFee` (UInt16): Transfer fee value; zero removes the field
- `IssuerEncryptionKey` (Blob): 33-byte EC-ElGamal public key for issuer
- `AuditorEncryptionKey` (Blob): 33-byte EC-ElGamal public key for auditor
- `DomainID` (UInt256): Permissioned domain ledger entry ID

## Lock/Unlock Operations

**Global Freeze (all holders):**
- Omit the `Holder` field
- Set `tfMPTLock` (flag value: 1) to lock all balances
- Set `tfMPTUnlock` (flag value: 2) to unlock all balances
- Requires: "Can Lock" flag already enabled on the issuance

**Per-Holder Freeze:**
- Include `Holder` field with target account
- Set `tfMPTLock` or `tfMPTUnlock` flag
- Cannot combine with field updates in same transaction

## Capability-Setting Flags

These enable features and "cannot be disabled" once activated:

| Flag | Hex | Dec | Purpose |
|------|-----|-----|---------|
| `tfMPTSetCanLock` | 0x04 | 4 | Enable issuer lock/unlock power |
| `tfMPTSetRequireAuth` | 0x08 | 8 | Require holder authorization |
| `tfMPTSetCanEscrow` | 0x10 | 16 | Allow escrow placement |
| `tfMPTSetCanTrade` | 0x20 | 32 | Enable DEX/AMM trading |
| `tfMPTSetCanTransfer` | 0x40 | 64 | Allow transfers to non-issuers |
| `tfMPTSetCanClawback` | 0x80 | 128 | Enable issuer clawback authority |
| `tfMPTSetCanHoldConfidentialBalance` | 0x100 | 256 | Enable confidential transfers |

Multiple capability flags can be combined in one transaction.

## Critical Constraints

- Lock/unlock flags cannot be combined with field updates or capability-setting flags
- "Both `tfMPTLock` and `tfMPTUnlock` are set" produces `temINVALID_FLAG` error
- Cannot specify both `DomainID` and `Holder` simultaneously
- Cannot use `Holder` with encryption keys
- Non-zero transfer fee requires "Can Transfer" flag enabled

# Multi-Purpose Tokens (MPTs): Compliance Controls & Issuance Flags

## Compliance Controls Supported

**Allow-listing (Require Auth):**
"If this flag is enabled, holders must get explicit approval from the issuer before they can hold this token." This creates an allowlist mechanism for controlling who can participate.

**Clawback:**
The issuer can reclaim tokens from holders when the "Can Clawback" flag is enabled. This functionality "can be used to revoke them, or to reassign the tokens in case the holder lost the keys to their account."

**Per-Holder Freeze (Lock):**
Issuers can "lock and unlock a specific token holder's balance; while locked, it cannot increase or decrease except in payments directly to the issuer." This is equivalent to deep freeze on trust line tokens.

**Global Freeze:**
The issuer can "globally lock (freeze) all MPTs of a particular issuance" when authorized.

**Banning:**
The document doesn't explicitly mention banning specific addresses as a distinct compliance control.

## Issuance Flags

Two primary flags control compliance powers:
- **Can Lock:** Enables individual or global locking
- **Can Clawback:** Enables token clawback operations

Additionally, **Can Transfer** and **Require Auth** flags govern transferability and authorization requirements.

## Lifecycle Constraints

The document doesn't detail specific ordering constraints like opt-in requirements before authorization or balance conditions before unauthorization.

# MPT Payment Transaction Structure

## Prerequisite: MPTokenAuthorize

Before receiving MPTs, the holder must authorize the token. Here's the xrpl.js example:

```js
const authorizeTx = {
  TransactionType: 'MPTokenAuthorize',
  Account: receiver.address,
  MPTokenIssuanceID: mptIssuanceID
}
```

According to the documentation, "any account that wants to hold an MPT, whether sending or receiving, must opt in first" by submitting an MPTokenAuthorize transaction.

## Payment Transaction JSON Shape

The Payment transaction for sending an MPT has this structure:

```js
const paymentTx = {
  TransactionType: 'Payment',
  Account: sender.address,
  Destination: receiver.address,
  Amount: {
    mpt_issuance_id: mptIssuanceID,
    value: '100'
  }
}
```

## Key Details

- The `Amount` field uses a specific format with `mpt_issuance_id` and `value` properties (both strings)
- The example sends a value of `"100"` which, with an asset scale of 2, displays as `1.00` units
- Submission requires autofill and wallet signing: `await client.submitAndWait(paymentTx, { wallet: sender, autofill: true })`

# MPT RequireAuth Lifecycle - XLS-33 Precise Specification

## (1) Holder vs Issuer Authorization Order

**Mandatory holder-first submission:** The specification states: "It is important to note that the holder always must first submit the `MPTokenAuthorize` transaction before the issuer."

The holder submits without the `MPTokenHolder` field (self-authorization), creating a zero-balance `MPToken` object. Only then can the issuer submit `MPTokenAuthorize` with `MPTokenHolder` field specified to set authorization.

## (2) Authorized State Representation

Authorization is tracked via the `lsfMPTAuthorized` flag on the `MPToken` object itself. The specification defines this flag: "If set, indicates that the issuer has authorized the holder for the MPT."

The mere existence of an `MPToken` object (created by holder's first transaction) is distinct from authorization status—the object exists but remains unauthorized until the issuer sets this flag.

## (3) Per-Holder Lock Prerequisite

Yes, the `MPToken` object must exist before per-holder locking. The `MPTokenIssuanceSet` transaction with `MPTokenHolder` field specified locks "an individual balance of an individual MPT," implying the balance (the `MPToken` object) must already exist.

## (4) Global Lock Flag on MPTokenIssuance

When locking all holders without specifying `MPTokenHolder`, the `lsfMPTLocked` flag is set on the `MPTokenIssuance` object itself: "If set, indicates that all balances are locked."

## (5) Complete Field/Flag Lists

**MPTokenIssuanceCreate transaction fields:**
- `TransactionType` (55)
- `AssetScale`, `Flags`, `TransferFee`, `MaximumAmount`, `MPTokenMetadata`

**Flags:** `tfMPTCanLock`, `tfMPTRequireAuth`, `tfMPTCanEscrow`, `tfMPTCanTrade`, `tfMPTCanTransfer`, `tfMPTCanClawback`

**MPTokenIssuanceSet fields:**
- `TransactionType` (56)
- `MPTokenIssuanceID`
- `MPTokenHolder` (optional)
- `Flag` (required)

**Flags:** `tfMPTLock`, `tfMPTUnlock`

**MPTokenAuthorize fields:**
- `TransactionType` (57)
- `MPTokenIssuanceID`
- `MPTokenHolder` (optional, issuer-only)
- `Flag` (required)

**Flags:** `tfMPTUnauthorize`

**Clawback fields (MPT extension):**
- `MPTokenHolder` field added (required for MPT clawback)
- `amount` field extended to support MPT via `mpt_issuance_id`

# MPToken Flags

The MPToken ledger entry supports two flags:

| Flag Name | Hex Value | Purpose |
|-----------|-----------|---------|
| `lsfMPTLocked` | `0x00000001` | "indicates that the MPT owned by this account is currently locked and cannot be used in any XRP transactions other than sending value back to the issuer" |
| `lsfMPTAuthorized` | `0x00000002` | Signals that an issuer has authorized the token holder for the MPT in allow-listing scenarios; can be toggled via `MPTokenAuthorize` transaction |

The project is complete and verified. Here's a summary:

**Module** (`src/mptIssuer.ts`) — a strict-TypeScript `MptIssuer` class wrapping XRPL Multi-Purpose Token transactions (`MPTokenIssuanceCreate`, `MPTokenIssuanceSet`, `MPTokenAuthorize`, `Clawback`, `Payment`) with:
- **Allowlist** — `optIn`/`approveHolder`/`revokeHolderApproval`, backed by the `RequireAuth` flag
- **Clawback** — `clawback`/`clawbackAll`
- **Bans** — `ban()` = clawback to zero + revoke allowlist authorization, so a banned address holds nothing and can't be paid again
- **Per-holder freeze** — `freezeHolder`/`unfreezeHolder`
- **Global freeze** — `globalFreeze`/`globalUnfreeze`
- Status reads (`getHolderStatus`, `getIssuanceStatus`) via direct `ledger_entry` lookups

One important finding from testing against real testnet behavior: XRPL's MPT "lock" (both per-holder and global) only blocks *peer-to-peer* transfers on-ledger — rippled still lets the issuer pay or debit a locked holder directly, mirroring legacy trust-line freeze semantics. Since the task requires a frozen holder to be fully blocked and global freeze to stop *all* movement, `pay()` adds an application-level guard (`MptComplianceError`) enforcing that on top of the ledger's own protection.

**Demo** (`src/demo.ts`, run via `npm run demo`) exercised every control against testnet, including negative tests (frozen holder blocked from sending/receiving, banned address blocked from receiving, payment blocked during global freeze), and asserted the exact final state.

Final verified ledger state (independently re-queried, not just from the script's own assertions):
- Issuance `0142AC97CA66BD5677AF4486998CF9F631F27FEA9BB3C1C4`: allowlist, clawback, and lock all enabled; not globally locked
- A: authorized, unfrozen, balance 500
- B: authorized, **frozen**, balance 700 (1000 sent, 300 clawed back)
- C: **unauthorized** (banned), balance 0 (250 sent, then fully clawed back)

`result.json` is written with the issuance ID and the three holder addresses. Note: the issuer account's testnet balance was topped up via the faucet during debugging (now ~105 XRP) since several iterations were needed to pin down real ledger behavior — no action needed on your end.
